I would really like to try and foster a sense of community on here because there is a social niche for the workforce and for students but they are subtractive rather than additive when you put them together - you can't go to on-campus programs because you have work - you can't stay late to help your team with the inventory deadline because you have a test to study for - that sort of thing. I'm going to drop a handful of relevant ice-breakers here.

  1. Why are you in school?
  2. What are you studying? Why?
  3. What kind of work do you do?
  4. Survival Factor: One job? More than one job? Flexible hours? Enough hours? Too many? Are you making enough to make ends meet? Are you making enough to flourish in at least a relative way?
  5. Do you share my disclosed sense of alienation or do you feel totally different about your situation?

Feel free to ask more questions that you want to see appended here. Feel free to answer ones I didn't ask that seem relevant! Also, hi!
Subverse Introductions: Who are you and why do you do what you do?

1. Because I want to create a better environment for my nearly 50 year working life and not work in shit retail forever.
  2. Biochemistry! Well at first I liked drugs, and then I liked science. Now I just friggin' love it. I can't explain why, something about being able to alter matter to get an end product makes me feel like a wizard.
  3. I was an auto-mechanic (low-level), now I fortunately got a killer job doing something involving the FDA.
  4. Was at two jobs, currently at one. (Thank god). Yes I am making enough to make ends meet and then some (finally), things are still really tight and I have to be diligent, but all in all I'm not eating cans of fucking beans so I'm happy.
  5. I definitely felt a sense of alienation. Without a doubt. I'm a pretty self-assured person, but when I was working my ass off both in school and work (now it's a bit more mild), I looked enviously on kids who either had their education paid for by the government or by their parents. I was in a weird limbo where I didn't qualify for financial aid and my parents excommunicated me in a sense. Turning 24 really, really, REALLY helped my situation. But at a time, I didn't feel like there was a light at the end of the tunnel. Like I was working hard and not being rewarded. I read every personal finance book I could get my hands on, thinking that I just wasn't "money-savvy" or was doing something wrong. I wasn't. It's a near impossibility to afford living and school simultaneously.

You and I have a lot in common, I think. Unfortunately by the time I turned 24 I had fucked up too much to get any FAFSA until I transfer out of community college. I'm still in that limbo of kind of hating other young people but I like the sense of legitimacy that comes with doing what I do more than I like the idea of jealously hungering after what they have - I think that just makes me arrogant. Also, I have totally thought about biochemistry for the same reasons and am totally into computer science for the sense of wizardry.

I literally JUST transferred out of my community college (Skyline College). Out of high school I got accepted to a lot of high end schools, I had a 4.2, Honors, AP, Academic Decathlon, etc. But my parents were just then on the brink of financial collapse and couldn't afford any of them and as an almost 18 year old, I had no idea what I was doing. Community college was an amazing experience for me. I felt like I had teachers who were actually invested in what I was doing with my life. So that definitely steered me towards biochemistry. I've always been a techie though! I actually code quite a bit on the side, have done a little web development and the such. Computer science is a badass field.

!!! I used to live right by the 120 and 121 SamTrans to Skyline. I scraped my way into the local state school at some point, went down to a polytechnical college in Sunnyvale that was great on paper but demoralizing in real life, plus I realized I was in Sunnyvale, fled back to the city at which point my parents were at the point of financial collapse for reasons thankfully unrelated to my collegiate mistakes. Community college has been a huge saving grace and has been a much more positive experience for me academically and in terms of support than Local-State-School ever was. (Although it certainly did have a lot of that "college experience" they tell you about and I'm grateful to have had a "freshman year"!) I also think BioChem is a badass field so there's a lot of internet high-fiving going on here. I pretty much only made it through high school because my high school was trash, though. I've spent years getting my shit together and as it stands I'm still working the retail game through school. (At least, until I get the IT associate's along with the CS associate's for transfer. Planning!)

I take a lot of comfort in the fact that many of my peers have no interest or motivation to move forward. As long as we keep inching forward, eventually we'll reach the mile mark. :P Now we just have to find others like us to get on this subreddit haha
